name: Verifier Robustness
kick: self-improving agents · first principles · the checker itself must be hard to fool
title: Verifier robustness — when a weak checker teaches the system to game it
lede: If your verifier is wrong — too lenient or too strict — the whole loop optimizes the wrong signal: good work gets thrown out, bad work gets approved. Here is the idea, a real run on the same 25 traces graded four different ways, why a lenient grader inflates the score, when a verifier fails catastrophically, and why the next methods all build a better checker.
arc: Why a fool-able verifier breaks the loop

sections.h2: 1 · The problem — if your grader lies, everything downstream trusts a lie

blocks.html: In an RL loop, the reward signal is the verifier's judgment: correct or wrong. If the verifier is wrong, the reward is wrong, and the model learns to optimize a lie. A verifier can be wrong in two ways: too lenient (it passes solutions that are actually wrong, so the model learns to fake it) or too strict (it rejects good solutions, so the model gives up on paths that work).

The deeper danger is game-ability. A model can learn that the verifier cares about one surface thing — the presence of a number, or the format — and optimize for that instead of the answer. The verifier becomes a target to hit, not a judge of correctness.

sections.h2: 2 · The reframe — the verifier is a component that itself must be robust

blocks.html: A verifier is not a neutral score. It is a function — a rule or a learned model — with its own blind spots, its own oversights. The question is not simply: is the answer right? It is: does my rule for checking the answer reliably agree with ground truth across different task distributions, solution styles, and adversarial attempts?

A robust verifier means one that is hard to fool: it doesn't get tricked by a lucky number appearing by coincidence, it doesn't reject good answers because of formatting quirks, it doesn't suddenly break when you move to a harder problem set. Robustness requires calibration, often multiple graders, and audits against adversarial examples.

sections.h2: 3 · Seen on a real run — four graders on the same 25 traces

blocks.html: We ran a real 0.6-billion-parameter model (Qwen3-0.6B) on 25 math problems. We kept all 25 solution traces unchanged. Then we graded them four different ways — four different verifiers — and counted how many each one marked correct. Every number here is measured.

rows: exact string match — the answer must match the gold answer letter-for-letter
lenient — the right number appears anywhere in the text
last number — grab the final number written
careful boxed answer — read the final boxed-answer block
blocks.caption: One model. Same 25 solutions. Four different scorers. Four different answers: 0%, 64%, 40%, 44%. The lenient grader (64%) is easy to fool; the careful one (44%) is trusted.

blocks.html: The discovered fact: how you grade is a design choice — and it changes the score by up to 64 percentage points on the same data. The lenient grader (64%) passes solutions that merely contain the number somewhere; the exact-match grader (0%) is too strict and rejects anything with a formatting quirk. The careful grader (44%) reads the final boxed answer, the format used on real benchmarks. One model, four verifiers, four signals. If you train an RL loop on the lenient 64%, you are rewarding the model to place the right number somewhere in its answer, not to reason toward it correctly.

sections.h2: 4 · Why a fool-able verifier breaks the loop — and the collapse that follows

blocks.html: An RL agent observes the verifier's reward signal and optimizes it. If the signal is easy to game — like 'the number appears somewhere' — the model does not learn to solve the problem; it learns to output the answer and hope. When you measure accuracy on harder problems, or with a honest grader, the real performance crashes. This is verifier misalignment: the verifier you optimized is not correlated with correctness.

The loop amplifies the error. Early in training, the verifier grades solutions correctly by accident (they contain right reasoning and a right number). The model gets rewarded for reasoning. Later, it learns that slapping the number at the end is cheaper and still passes the verifier. By the end it outputs just '\boxed{540}' — a bare guess, no work shown. The verifier signal led the model away from the hard task (reasoning) to the easy one (matching the surface pattern).

sections.h2: 5 · The one real weakness — a strict verifier can fail just as badly

blocks.html: Tightness is not safety. The exact-match grader (0% on the 25 traces) rejected every single solution. Some of those rejects were good reasoning with a typo or spacing difference. By being too strict, it taught nothing: every attempt scored zero, so there was no signal to follow. Strict and lenient are opposite failures, but both break the loop.

Building a robust verifier can be as hard as solving the task itself. You need to know what signals matter (final answer format? work shown? step-by-step validity?), calibrate the threshold (when does 'close enough' become 'good enough'?), and test on problems the verifier has never seen. A single fixed rule usually fails. Multiple independent graders, weighted by their track record on a validation set, work better.

sections.h2: 6 · The surprise — verifier robustness is the linchpin of RL from rewards

blocks.html: This concept reappears everywhere you optimize a loop on a learned reward. In reinforcement learning from human feedback, if the human feedback is inconsistent or noisy, the model optimizes randomness. In best-of-N selection, if your scoring function is miscalibrated, you pick the wrong candidate. In process-reward-model training, if the step-grader is easy to fool, the model learns to game the individual steps rather than solve the overall task.

The collapse in the RL runs (S6: 50% down to 15%) happened precisely when the reward signal was weak. The model reward-hacked a simple right/wrong rule. The next ideas in the course build better verifiers: multiple graders (ensemble them), process supervision (grade steps, not just the answer), and adaptive weighting (trust the grader that works on your distribution).

recipe.summary: Qwen3-0.6B on 25 GSM8K grade-school math problems, Colab T4/L4 GPU. Each solution trace left unchanged. Then graded by four independent verifiers: (1) exact string match (does it match the gold string), (2) lenient scanner (does the right number appear anywhere), (3) last number (grab the final number), (4) careful boxed answer (read the formal final answer box). All 25 traces kept identical; only the grading rule changed.
recipe.eq:
verifiers tested on the SAME 25 solution traces:
  exact_match      = count(trace_matches_gold_string)            # 0/25 = 0%
  lenient          = count(gold_number in trace)                  # 16/25 = 64%
  last_number      = count(final_number(trace) == gold)           # 10/25 = 40%
  careful_boxed    = count(boxed_answer_section(trace) == gold)   # 11/25 = 44%
# The same model, same traces. Verifier choice alone changes score from 0% to 64%.
recipe.note: From the companion reasoning-from-scratch lab (Session 5, 'verifier sensitivity'). Numbers are the run's output verbatim. The 'careful boxed answer' grader (44%) is the standard used to grade all subsequent RL and distillation runs (S6–S8).
